Radar cross section (RCS) reduction is crucial for stealth technology in military applications.
Passive techniques for RCS reduction include shaping and radar absorbing materials (RAM).
Active techniques for RCS reduction include active cancellation and passive cancellation.
Polarization conversion metamaterial (PCM) can reduce in-band RCS by up to 16 dB compared to a reference antenna.
Frequency selective surfaces (FSS) can achieve broadband RCS reduction by blocking or passing specific frequency bands.
Artificial magnetic conductors (AMC) can achieve RCS reduction with a bandwidth of up to 93%.
Composite AMC surfaces use two types of AMC cells operating at different frequencies to cancel out reflections.
The chessboard surface structure with two AMC cells achieves -10 dB RCS reduction over 73% of the frequency bandwidth.
Microstrip resonators can achieve in-band RCS reduction by modifying the antenna's electromagnetic response.
Radar absorbing materials (RAM) convert incident electromagnetic energy into heat, reducing reflected energy.
RAM effectiveness depends on the angle of incidence, frequency, and polarization of the incident wave.
Active cancellation involves emitting a signal out of phase with the reflected wave to reduce radar return.
Shaping reduces RCS by deflecting scattered energy away from the radar, minimizing specular reflections.
The RCS of an object depends on its shape, size, material properties, and the ratio of its dimensions to the wavelength of the incident radar wave.
Metamaterials can miniaturize antennas, expand their operating band, enhance gain, and reduce RCS.
The proposed metamaterial unit cell consists of a square loop and intersecting strips at the edges.
Metamaterials are artificial materials with unique electromagnetic properties not found in nature.
Negative-index metamaterials (NIM) have a negative index of refraction due to negative values of both permeability and permittivity.
Chiral metamaterials have non-zero effective parameter k and can support left-handed and right-handed circularly polarized waves.
Electromagnetic band gap (EBG) metamaterials control light propagation and can be designed with band gaps at desired frequencies.
Frequency selective surfaces (FSS) are periodic surfaces that can block or pass electromagnetic waves at specific frequencies.
FSS can be designed with fractal elements, active and three-dimensional structures, and embedded plates and rods.
Integrated FSS structures combine multiple layers and materials for enhanced performance.
The efficiency of passive RCS reduction techniques depends on the angle of incidence, frequency, and polarization of the incident wave.
Modern radar systems span a wide range of frequencies, requiring broadband RCS reduction techniques.
